content_metadata.description: A guided virtual exploration of asteroid Vesta using 3D models and close-up views, narrated by a female voice.

qAndA.answer: A set of troughs that ring the equator.
qAndA.question: What is the most distinctive feature that separates Vesta's northern and southern hemispheres?

qAndA.answer: The Marcia crater. It's significant because it's a fairly recent impact that reveals deeper material excavated to the surface.
qAndA.question: What is the name of the large crater located in Vesta's northern hemisphere, and what makes it significant?

qAndA.answer: Slumping, where material has moved downslope, revealing fresher material underneath.
qAndA.question: What geological process is evident in the features surrounding the central mound in Vesta's south polar basin?

qAndA.answer: It's about two and a half times the height of Mount Everest.
qAndA.question: How does the height of the central mound in Vesta's south polar basin compare to Mount Everest on Earth?

qAndA.answer: The video starts with a mood of curiosity and transitions to excitement as it reveals more fascinating details about Vesta. The narrator's enthusiastic tone, especially when describing the central mound, contributes to the overall sense of wonder and excitement.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Put on your 3D glasses and let's take a look at Vesta.
This is Asteroid Vesta, a remnant protoplanet from the beginning of the solar system.
It's a very large, oblate asteroid about 530 kilometers in diameter.
And what you see here is that it's separated north to south by a set of troughs that ring the equator.
This is a very unusual feature that we're very interested in studying.
In the north of Vesta, there's a large set of craters that we call the snowman.
And this one at the bottom, this large crater is named Marcia.
It's a fairly recent crater that shows evidence of deeper material that has been excavated to the surface.
And here we're looking at the South Polar Basin, the central mound,
which is one of the largest mountains in the solar system,
and about 2.5 times the height of Mount Everest on the earth.
It's a cratered mound, and also shows many features where material has slumped,
And here we can see one of those slumps and the scarps in the distance.
This mound is very unusual. It has many grooves and lineations that were very interested in studying.
We're really excited that Don is on its way to its lowest altitude.

The last few seconds are missing from this version. A corrected version is available at http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zudzwjw7wRE

Converted NASA/JPLNews' Video to side-by-side youtube 3d video with ffmpeg and imagemagick using only the red and green channels. The blue channel has been dropped all together. Source Video taken from:
http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/video/download.php?mm_type=hdmov&id=1041&file=dawn/20111201/dawn20111130-1280.mov
http://www.jpl.nasa.gov/video/
http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/dawn/news/dawn20111201.html 
http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGpZT8WL2y0


The following script was used to create this video. Sadly, ffmpeg segfaults reproducably close to the end, so the Video is cut short by a few seconds.
#!/bin/bash
#ffmpeg  -i  dawn20111201-1280.mov  -vcodec png -an 1_png/dawn%d.png
#ffmpeg -i dawn20111201-1280.mov  -f matroska -vn -y dawn_aac.mkv
# mkdir 8
# mkdir 2_rg
# mkdir 1_png

for i in 1_png/*png; do 
   B=`basename "$i" .png`
   r=2_rg/"$B"_r.png
   g=2_rg/"$B"_g.png
   #s=3_s/"$B"_s.png
   s=8/"$B"_s.png
   convert "$i" -channel R -separate "$r"; 
   convert "$i" -channel G -separate "$g"

   #convert -size 1280x720 xc:magenta -draw  "image SrcOver 0,0 640,720 \"${r}\"" -draw "image SrcOver 640,0 640,720 \"${g}\""  "${s}"
   #for i in 3_s/*_s.png; do convert -depth 8 $i  8/`basename $i .png`8.png; done
   #for i in 3_s/*_s.png; do convert -depth 8 $i  8/`basename $i .png`8.png; done

   convert -size 1280x720 xc:magenta -draw  "image SrcOver 0,0 640,720 \"${r}\"" -draw "image SrcOver 640,0 640,720 \"${g}\"" -depth 8  "${s}"
   #for i in 3_s/*_s.png; do convert -depth 8 $i  8/`basename $i .png`8.png; done

   echo -n .
done
time ffmpeg -i 8/dawn%d_s8.png -i dawn_aac.mkv -r 29.970 -f matroska -vcodec libx264  -vpre libx264-medium -acodec copy  -b 9176k -refs 1 -keyint_min 25   -y dawn_3d_2.mkv
